texto: Writing this review at midnight so… I tried following along with Pump It Up as I watched it and dislocated my leg, this is ridiculous, I want a refund. 0/10. A grotesquely made satire, that can be best described as equal parts gross, depressing, funny, and raunchy. Demi Moore and Margaret Qualley brought a lot to this, playing Elisabeth/Sue playing the dual identities to feel like the same person (after all they are one) but different enough to feel distinct. Dennis Quaid is great at playing the most disgusting part of the movie, Harvey. The real star of the show here is Fargeat’s directing. A visual and audial treat of a movie. Not a treat like candy but the talent on display is stunning and I hope she continues making more movies (I also caught a bit of Revenge but not enough for a review). Stunning use of color and not to mention the creature and body horror effects. A lot of the creature stuff didn’t really freak me out but Elisabeth/Sue’s body mangling and decaying had mc flinching. There’s a bit to be said on the films similarities to the manga Helter Skelter and Oliver Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Grey. Which aren’t bad, nothing is original, and are distinct works but it’s interesting how they all handle the deterioration of self in search of beauty. How did Sue manage to build a small room in like, a few days. There’s a lot of heightened reality in this movie but that really took me out. I do think a few times the movie over explains its ideas, however that being said this is a thematically rich movie. The core is obvious, how women are treated within beauty standards, Elisabeth wants to maintain her youth and fame so she uses The Substance that’s the premise. The film shows that in a lot of ways how that’s enforced by men, Harvey’s introduction has him reference fertility ages, a note Elisabeth receives says “you WERE amazing, and when she interacts with the biker as Elisabeth and not as Sue, he yells at her. Harvey and the executives even say “pretty girls should always smile” before running off to chase dancers like dogs. Sue also enforces this. Giving Elisabeth an astronomically high standard, she cannot meet, although they are one. Both versions of Pump It Up are a good point here— Elisabeth’s show is mostly in a wideshot, instructions pretty clear. The leotard more of a cloth texture, though fitting, isn’t painted on. Then you have Sue’s… which is different. It’s a male gaze wet dream, a metallic bikini that’s practically spray painted on, is basically a thong on the bottom, and is cut to the point it can barely be considered athletic wear. It’s enforced on Elisabeth largely and more subtly on Sue. Funnily enough by the end, once everything goes wrong, that’s the only way the two could escape the cage of beauty standards. Two other threads I read in the film is within “respect the balance” is about self hatred and work life balance. Which going from male gaze to love yourself in theme is a leap but— Elisabeth and Sue hate eachother one considering her a “selfish bitch” the other an old woman who wastes her life. Yet they are the same person, they are one. Sue forces herself to work at Elisabteh’s expense, and Elisabeth does nothing in the meantime, just waiting for more Sue time. She buried herself in her career, and neglected any sort of relationships, that being familial, friendly, or otherwise. Her self-worth is her career, that’s all she has. And if she doesn’t have a career, she doesn’t have a self. Which she hates. While I just went on this whole thing about self hatred within the fact that though they are the same person Elisabeth and Sue hate eachother. I do think strangely enough, though it contradicts they have something that reads as a deeply messed up mother and daughter relationship. I think most of this comes from the interview scene. Elisabeth finds Sue spoiled, someone she gave life, someone who owes everything to her, and stealing away what she had. Sue thinks Elisabeth is jurassic, old, remarking she didn’t like the show but it was “inescapable”. Which does read a lot like a mother and daughters, not to so positive opinion of one another. It could be said that Elisabeth is exploiting the girl she created to extend her career, live through her, in this case literally. Though that does sort of ignore that Sue is defintley an extension of Elisabeth’s narcissism. Within that there’s two ways I see the Elisabeth/Sue fight. It’s either a manifestation of self hatred or a daughter trying to be her own person. Decide which one you like more, don’t debate in the comments. I do think the ending is far more campy than the first two hours but it’s not bad, a bloody wild climax. Anyways I’m glad to say The Substance has… The Substance in terms of theme and what it’s trying to say. Can’t wait to see whatever Fargeat does next, and though I’m not looking forward to it, I hope Demi Moore gets more work in the future, I’m sure Margaret Qualley will do great in the Posession remake.

texto: Whoa!! This is awesome. Totally insane body horror of the highest order. Filled with the most gratuitously sexual shots of female bodies AND also the most disgustingly gross shots of [redacted] female bodies. It's entertaining as hell! Though the story isn't necessarily anything original (being obsessed with beauty always leads to misery) but the way it's told in THIS film is original. Horror fans are going to lose their shit for this. Rare to see the Cannes press screening audience go THIS wild during a film - that's always the mark of something truly great. If Coralie Fargeat could trim this down by 20 minutes and cut out some of the unnecessarily repetitive shots, this would be an all-timer. It's that close.

texto: This film is gonna be a huge divider. All I know is: I won't forget that screening in a hurry. Every Cannes has one: a love it or hate it title that becomes a word-of-mouth sensation thanks to the sheer division it creates among festivalgoers. No, we’re not talking about the so-bad-it-still-isn’t-good Megalopolis, but The Substance, a body horror that goes places even body horror aficionados will be shocked by. Helping this film’s cause are a few things – firstly, it’s the second film from Coralie Fargeat, whose gory thriller Revenge marked her out as one to watch back in 2017 – but, secondly it marks a return-of-sorts for 1990s icon Demi Moore, who is fantastically cast as an ageing Hollywood star who takes a black market drug to create a younger version of herself. The Substance is as gruesome as they come, culminating with an extended sequence that needs to be experienced with a crowd.
